newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright seeks out tragic Jewish roots in Prague.
newsitem.headline: Albright seeks out tragic Jewish roots in Prague.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright sought out her Jewish roots on Sunday at the start of an emotional visit to her native city of Prague.

Albright, on a private tour of the ancient Jewish quarter in the Czech capital, was shown the names of her paternal grandparents on the walls of a synagogue dedicated to the memory of more than 77,000 Czechoslovak Jews who perished in Nazi concentration camps in World War Two.

Albright, who only recently became aware of her Jewish ancestry, visited the Pinkas Synagogue with U.S. First Lady Hilllary Clinton about a year ago but had not realised her grandparents, Arnost Korbel and his wife Olga, were among the names which cover the inside walls.

"Tonight I knew to look for those names and their image will for ever be seared into my heart," Albright said in a statement delivered outside the Jewish Town Hall, the centre of Prague's Jewish community.

"Now that I am aware of my own Jewish background, that my grandparents died in concentration camps, the evil of the Holocaust has an even more personal meaning for me and I feel an even greater determination to ensure that it will never be forgotten," she said, her voice cracking with emotion.

Albright, dressed in a black suit with a sun-shaped brooch, also examined a card from an index kept in the Town Hall, which showed Arnost and Olga Korbel were admitted to Terezin (Theresienstadt in German) camp on July 30, 1942.
Her grandfather died within six weeks. His wife was transported to Auschwitz camp in Poland and died in October 1944.
Albright was born Marie Jana Korbelova in Prague in 1937. Her father, Josef Korbel, was a Czechoslovak diplomat. From an early age she believed she had been raised a Roman Catholic.
However, the Washington Post, researching her background earlier this year, found she appeared to be of Jewish ancestry and that three of her grandparents had died in the Holocaust.
Albright's family was forced to flee Czechoslovakia twice, once to escape the Nazis and then, in 1948, the Communists.
"As I stood looking at that melancholy wall, I not only grieved for those members of my family whose names are inscribed there, but I also thought about my parents.

"I thought about the choice they made. They clearly confronted the most excruciating decision a human being can face when they left members of their family behind even as they saved me from certain death...that most painful of choices gave me life a second time."
Soon after her ancestry was revealed, Albright said she would deal with the issue in a personal way.
"To the many values and many facets that make up who I am, I now add the knowledge that my grandparents and members of my family perished in the worst catastrophe in human history.

"So I leave here tonight with the certainty that this new part of my identity adds something stronger, sadder and richer to my life," she said, before turning and walking up the narrow street into the darkness.
Leo Pavlat, the director of Prague's Jewish Museum, said Albright's emotion was natural.
"She is not here for the first time, but it is the first time she came with the aim to look at the names." he said.
"But all people who come here for the first time and find the names of their relatives are moved. That is a human thing, regardless of their position," he added.

Albright's tour, which included a visit to the Old Jewish Cemetery of up to 100,000 graves, was not part of her official programme beginning on Monday and was witnessed by only a few Jewish tourists who happened to be in the area.
